Sample text:
---
# In Praise of Maps That Are Wrong

There is a map from 1570, made by the Flemish cartographer Abraham Ortelius, that shows a vast southern continent stretching across the bottom of the world. It has coastlines, capes, and bays with names. Nobody had ever seen it. It was a guess, an inference dressed as a fact: the world seemed like it ought to be balanced, so the mapmakers gave the south a landmass to counterweight the north. For two centuries, explorers went looking for *Terra Australis*, and some of them nearly died trying to find it.

I love this map, and I love it more because it is wrong.

## The confidence of the blank

We tend to think of old maps as charming failures: sea serpents curling around ships, cartouches held up by chubby cherubs, mountains drawn like rows of molehills. But the sea serpents are not the most interesting feature. The most interesting feature is the mapmaker's problem with emptiness.

Empty space on a map is uncomfortable. A blank patch says *I don't know*, and a map that says *I don't know* is, commercially and socially, a weak map. So cartographers filled the gaps. Sometimes they filled them with monsters, which at least were honest about being decorative. Sometimes they filled them with rivers that hadn't been traced, or mountain ranges copied from rumor, or an entire island, California, drawn floating off the coast of North America for over a hundred years because a few influential maps insisted on it.

What strikes me is that none of this was exactly lying. It was the best available synthesis of fragmentary reports. A sailor said he'd seen land. Another said the coast bent west. A third had a story from a man who had it from a trader. The mapmaker's job was to reconcile these into a single image, and a single image has to commit. You cannot draw a maybe. A line is either there or it isn't.

That, I think, is the deep tension in all knowledge. The world does not come in probabilities, but our pictures of it must, at some point, become definite enough to use.

## Wrongness as a working tool

Here is what I find moving: the wrong maps worked. Not perfectly, and not everywhere, but they did what a map is for. They gave people something to steer by. The imaginary southern continent pulled ships toward the bottom of the world, and although they didn't find the continent Ortelius drew, they found Australia, and New Zealand, and eventually Antarctica, which really is a southern continent, just far colder, far smaller than the fantasy, and far less hospitable to a merchant's dreams.

The error was productive. It made a claim specific enough to be tested. Captain Cook sailed south in the 1770s largely to settle the question, and by failing to find the great fertile land, he *corrected the map*. That correction only became possible because someone had first been bold enough to draw the thing wrong.

Compare that with a map left honestly blank. A blank map can never be disproved. It also never sends anyone anywhere.

I don't want to push this too far. There is a real cost to false confidence, and plenty of people suffered from bad charts: ships wrecked on reefs that weren't marked, armies marching toward rivers that weren't there. But the lesson isn't "be wrong freely." It's subtler. A good map is one that can be revised, and it stays revisable only if someone treats it as a claim rather than a monument.

## The map is not the territory, but we forget

The philosopher Alfred Korzybski gave us the phrase "the map is not the territory," and it has been quoted so often it has gone slightly smooth, like a stone in a river. But the idea keeps being worth rediscovering, because we keep forgetting it.

We forget it whenever we mistake a model for the thing it models. An economic forecast becomes "what will happen." A personality type becomes "who this person is." A diagnosis, a category, a headline, a résumé: all of them are maps, useful compressions, and all of them leave out nearly everything. The danger is never that we use maps. We can't do otherwise. The danger is the moment we stop feeling the edges, when the coastline on the page starts to seem more real than the coast.

The old cartographers, oddly, may have been better at this than we are. They knew their maps were provisional. They wrote things like *Hic sunt dracones*, or its many cousins, "here be dragons," a phrase that is almost certainly more legend than practice (it appears on only a couple of surviving artifacts), but that captures a real attitude. At the edge of what you know, you mark the edge. You say something, even if the something is a dragon.

## What I'd want from my own maps

If I think about my own understanding of the world, it is a chart of this kind. Some regions are surveyed carefully, with soundings and cross-checked bearings. Others are sketched from hearsay. A few, if I'm honest, are pure Ortelius: a tidy continent I've drawn because the world felt like it needed one there.

What I'd want, then, is not a map without errors, which is impossible, but a map with honest margins. I'd want the surveyed coast drawn in firm ink and the rumored coast drawn dotted. I'd want to be able to say "this is what I think is there, and here is how I came to think it," so that the next traveler, or the next version of me, knows where to check first.

Some modern maps do this well. Nautical charts print the date of the survey, and the oldest soundings are flagged as unreliable. Geological maps distinguish between *observed* and *inferred* boundaries with solid and dashed lines. It is a small typographic humility, a dash instead of a line, and I think it may be one of the most intellectually honest gestures we have.

## The dragon at the edge

I keep coming back to that imaginary southern continent. There's something almost tender in it. A whole generation of thinkers looked at the unknown bottom of the world and reasoned, from symmetry and hope, that something large and green must be waiting. They were wrong about the shape of the answer but right that there was an answer. The wrongness was a kind of reaching.

Maybe that's the best defense of a wrong map: it is what curiosity looks like once it has to put pen to paper. To draw is to risk. The people who drew coastlines they'd never seen were, in their way, the ancestors of every scientist who has written a hypothesis down where others could shoot at it.

So here's to the wrong maps, the floating Californias and the phantom continents. They were not the opposite of knowledge. They were knowledge in its awkward adolescence, committed enough to be corrected, and brave enough to be wrong on paper, where someone could sail out and find out.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A polished, metaphor-driven reflection whose recurring map imagery gives its argument a distinct personal voice.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, assured, and willing to complicate its own thesis: wrong maps can be generative, but false confidence has real costs. Its pathos comes from treating error not as a failure to know, but as a vulnerable act of reaching that can be tested and revised. The essay invites readers to hold their own models lightly—to mark what is inferred, admit what is unknown, and remain curious enough to draw a provisional map.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample centers on imagined continents, blank spaces, dashed lines, and the difference between a map and the territory. It connects cartographic errors to scientific hypotheses and everyday categories, foregrounding intellectual humility, curiosity, and correction as conditions of useful knowledge.

## Evidence line
> A good map is one that can be revised, and it stays revisable only if someone treats it as a claim rather than a monument.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive metaphor across historical examples and personal reflection, repeatedly favoring revisability and candid uncertainty over the appearance of certainty.
